documents.label: Personality, Strengths & Blind Spots
documents.body: My Personality Profile Myers-Briggs: ENTJ-A ("The Commander") Big Five / OCEAN: Very high Conscientiousness (108) & Extraversion (106); very low Agreeableness (61) & Neuroticism (38). As in, top 1-5% most extreme for all four 😅 Gallup CliftonStrengths: My dominant themes are in the Influencing and Executing domains. Image Achiever: I work hard and possess a great deal of stamina. I take immense satisfaction in being busy and productive. I love to complete tasks, and my accomplishments fulfill me. I have a strong inner drive — an innate source of intensity, energy and power that motivates me to work hard to get things done. Arranger: I can organize, but also have a flexibility that complements this ability. I like to determine how all of the pieces and resources can be arranged for maximum productivity. I have a natural ability to coordinate people and resources for maximum effectiveness. My creative flexibility in complex situations leads to greater efficiency. Learner: I have a great desire to learn and want to continuously improve. The process of learning, rather than the outcome, excites me. I provide your teammates with a logical perspective on things. Competition: I measure my progress against the performance of others. I strive to win first place and revel in contests. I motivate yourself and others to a higher standard of performance. I can raise a group’s achievement level by creating a culture of winning and aspiring to be the best. Significance: I want to make a big impact. I am independent and prioritize projects based on how much influence they will have on your organization or people around me. I want to do important work and are determined to make a difference. I want others to respect me for my significant contribution and willingness to work hard to achieve success. BIS-11: Very low impulsiveness (41). In practice, this means: I am a mission-oriented systems-builder energized by ambitious goals and rational debate. I thrive on turning chaos into order and driving a team toward a clear, world-changing objective. I view my (very) high disagreeableness as a feature of my commitment to my mission. I believe that intellectual honesty and rigorous debate are the fastest path to the best ideas. My Strengths My Gallup profile concentrates in Influencing and Executing – but my impact comes from how these combine with my drive for Significance. You should leverage me accordingly. Influencing ~ "the catalyst" First-principles: I love rigorous, first-principles debate. I build cases methodically and am effective at rallying alignment behind a mission. Inspiring action: I articulate compelling visions that energize teams and partners. Taking charge: I love stepping into chaos, making tough calls, and creating clarity where there is none. I thrive under pressure. Executing ~ "the architect" Making things happen: My instinct is to turn ideas into action. I have a deep-seated need to see tangible progress every day. Organizing complexity: I break down large, complex challenges into elegant systems and processes. This is where my obsession with systems-building lives. Raising the bar: I create cultures of winning – measuring progress, celebrating milestones, and pushing the team toward a higher standard. Strategic thinking ~ "the philosopher" Learning & synthesizing: I am a relentless learner, constantly pulling ideas from disparate fields to find integrative insights. Seeing the future: I often live 1-3 years ahead, anticipating challenges and opportunities before they arrive. Holding paradoxes: I often hold two opposing ideas in tension and still act decisively. Integrative thinking is a core skill. Relationship-building ~ "the connector" Superconnector: I love mapping social graphs and making catalytic introductions that create value for all involved. Culture creator: I design rituals, spaces, and shared experiences that compound trust and belonging over time. Coalition builder: I align talent, capital, and culture behind one mission – and create co-ownership so wins feel shared. My Blind Spots (Where I Need Your Help) I'm working to notice and correct these before they affect others. You are always invited (but never responsible) to flag them! If you name it, I will do my best to pause, understand the impact, and repair rather than defend it. Over-structured: I LOVE systems and process. But sometimes situations call for fluidity, improvisation, or just vibing – and I can be too rigid when looseness would serve better. Help me: "This one doesn't need a framework – let's just riff." Control creep: My default is to do it myself, especially on things I used to own. This makes me a bottleneck. Help me: Proactively own your domain. If I'm creeping into your weeds, say: "Chappy, I've got this. Let me come back with a finished product." I’ll recognize it as gift, not a challenge. Intensity: I have a high internal clock + can be overwhelming → I inadvertently judge or blame others for not keeping up. Help me: Tell me if my pace is unsustainable for you. High performance AND psychological safety aren't opposites. Stress spillover: When I'm underslept, dieting hard, overloaded, or frustrated, I can become tense, uncommunicative, abrasive, and harder to read. If I land sharply, I should pause, reset, and repair rather than expecting you to deal with it. Over-scheduled (120%): I tend to pack my todo list beyond capacity, leaving no slack for serendipity, spontaneous connection, or the unexpected opportunities that often matter most. Help me: If you see something worth my time, push for it.

documents.label: How We Collaborate
documents.body: My Time & Availability Working hours: I am effectively always working (usually 80-100 h/w 😅), but my core, most responsive hours are 9am-7pm PT. You can expect me to be highly engaged during this window. (Curious? Check out Chappy’s Core Daily Routine) Weekends: My mornings before 9am, as well as Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, are my protected deep work blocks (eg. coding, writing, researching, strategy). I will be slow to respond during these blocks. I work intensely on weekends, but I cherish this time for uninterrupted, creative deep work. Please respect this by avoiding non-urgent requests. Meetings Philosophy: I believe meetings are for two things: 1) high-bandwidth debate to solve a hard problem, and 2) efficient, team-wide status updates and alignment. Expectations: Come on time & prepared: I expect the meeting leader to arrive on time and with a clear (and ideally written) agenda. Active participation: I expect everyone on the call to be engaged and to contribute. The meeting leader is responsible for creating and facilitating these conditions. Pre-reads: A pre-read in advance before is a gift to everyone in the meeting – especially if it’s more of a homework assignment rather than passive read! It's by no means required, but it is always appreciated and allows us to use our synchronous time for the highest-value and most informed discussions.

documents.label: Communication
documents.body: Note on my response time: I am often juggling a very high volume (100+ of open lines. While I will see your message, it may occasionally take me 5-8 days to respond to non-urgent pings. Please do not take this personally; it is a function of my batching system for managing focus. If you need a faster response, read on! My Communication Principles Async-first: I believe the best work happens in long, uninterrupted blocks of focus. For any complex topic, my strong preference is to start with a written, well-structured document (like a Notion or Google Doc). This allows me to engage with your ideas deeply on my own schedule and it forces clarity of thought for everyone involved. High signal-to-noise ratio: Be concise. Use bullet points. Get to the point quickly and put your rec or key question at the top. I trust you've done the deep thinking; you don't need to show all your work in the initial message. Minimal ChatGPT fluff please! Context is your responsibility: Please ask "does Chappy have all the context he needs to make an informed decision on this?" If no, provide the necessary background docs / links. Reducing friction is the fastest way to get a response! Default to transparency: Whenever possible, our communications should happen in shared, public channels within the team. This reduces redundant conversations, creates a shared context, and allows others to learn and contribute. The Right Channel for the Job For non-urgent, day-to-day comms & FYIs: Use the appropriate public Slack channel. If you need my specific input, you must @ me or I will likely miss it. I am in over 100 channels (in AIC) and rely on mentions to filter what's important. To get my input on a document: Share a Notion or Google Doc with me and @ me in a specific channel with a clear question and your recommendation. This ensures it hits my radar. To pitch me a new, big idea: Write a concise, one-page document outlining: 1) the problem, 2) the proposed solution, and 3) a concrete first step. Share this with me via Slack. For an urgent, time-sensitive issue (≤ 3 hours): Send me a text message prefixed with "URGENT:". This will get my immediate attention. My phone # is included in my email signature and on my Slack profile.

documents.label: Feedback
documents.body: How to Give Me Feedback I am running a thousand miles an hour and am full of blind spots. Please help me see them! Your honest perspective is a gift that helps me and our shared mission get better. The method: (a https://books.chappyasel.com/crucial-conversations framework) Ask for permission: Because I am constantly context-switching, the most effective way to give me feedback is to first get my attention. A simple Slack message like, "Hey Chappy, do you have 10 minutes for some feedback on X later today?" is the perfect way to start. This allows me to switch into the right mental frame to actually hear you. Lead with the facts: Start with a neutral, specific observation. (eg. "In the leadership sync yesterday, when we discussed the budget, I noticed we moved to a decision without hearing from the broader team.") Share Your story: Explain the impact this had on you or the project. (eg. "The story I told myself was that we are prioritizing speed over rigor in our financial planning, which makes me concerned about future risks.") End with a question: Open the door for a real conversation. (eg. "I was hoping you could help me understand your thinking there?") How I Give Feedback My philosophy: (from https://books.chappyasel.com/radical-candor) I aim to care personally while challenging directly. I intend to address the work or behavior rather than the person, but intent doesn't determine impact. If I land badly or make an unfair inference, tell me! How I recognize great work I believe that recognition is a critical part of a high-performance culture. My goal is to ensure you feel seen and valued for your contributions. How I show it: Succinct public praise: I frequently give public praise for specific, excellent work, especially in our Slack channels or team meetings. My style is often succinct and direct, but it is a sincere acknowledgment of a job well done. Trust and autonomy: The single greatest way I show my respect for your work is by giving you more of it. When you consistently deliver with excellence, I will respond by giving you more ownership, more freedom, and bigger, more interesting problems to solve. Advocacy: I will champion you and your work in the rooms you are not in. I will use my network and my platform to create opportunities for you and to ensure your contributions are recognized by the people who matter. This is definitely a WIP and probably always will be! If we've worked closely together: What here matches your experience? What's missing or wrong? I care much more about making this true than making it flattering.

documents.label: Why So Early?
documents.body: Origin story: Growing up, I was very definitively a night owl. It wasn’t until cutting for my first bodybuilding competition in 2022 when my hormones got thrown completely out of whack that I started naturally / uncontrollably waking up at 4am, 3am, and sometimes even 2am wired 😅. Ever since mid-2022, I made the permanent transition to that earlier time and haven’t looked back! Why wake up extremely early? Here are a few of my favorites: It’s easy, actually It doesn’t really take any extraordinary willpower to wake up early! Fundamentally, I’m still sleeping the same amount as anyone else would, I’m just shifting my schedule earlier. Commit to it for a couple of weeks and watch your circadian rhythm naturally shift! I get 4+ hours completely to myself That give me time to grab full control of my schedule before anyone can disturb me! I try to allocate as much of this time as I can to “eating the frog” – working on the day’s biggest and most important project Once the meetings + comms bombardment starts, my plate gets filled up will small yet urgent tasks which can easily engulf the rest of my day I can’t miss a workout When I work out this early in the morning before all meeting, it’s nearly impossible to make an excuse to miss it (not that working out too little is ever an issue 😅) I only have to shower once There are naturally two points where I have to shower daily: once after my workout and once before my meetings. Why not line the two up?! I have enough time This gives me enough time to work out early in the morning, shower, and get going My benchmark is at least 4 hours between waking and first meeting. That’s the minimum I can fit my full morning routine into and not feel too rushed I naturally out-work everyone By starting work before 4am every morning, most people’s 9-5 becomes my 12-hour work day. The inertia naturally becomes that I out-work everyone!

documents.label: Sinusoidal vs Square-wave Alertness
documents.body: Taken from Why We Sleep, here’s how alertness naturally varies throughout the day: Image Given this, you could argue that alertness follows a sawtooth pattern throughout the day. However, I think most people actually experience a sinusoidal pattern of alertness. Finally, most people would probably tell you they desire a square-wave pattern of alertness if it were reasonably achievable. Image Here’s my best attempt at doing so! AM: Get the blood flowing, caffeine + ⍺-GPC, and artificial sun exposure ASAP PM: Sleep stack + melatonin (and a whole routine in general) to prime the body for sleep Make this your #1 priority!

documents.label: Sleep Duration
documents.body: Contrarian opinion: I think most people actually get too much sleep! Yes, I’ve read Why We Sleep which makes a statistically rigorous argument for 8+ hours daily. However, studies also show that anywhere between 6-8 hours works. In fact, all cause mortality with 8 hours is actually higher than with 5 hours: (caveat: correlation vs causation). Also, my father was a lifelong 4-6hrs/night sleeper so I might’ve inherited the gene from him! Image When I oversleep, I often feel more lethargic the following day yet have trouble going to sleep at the end of the night. I’ve found the right amount of sleep for me varies from anywhere between 5 hours and 7.5 hours (avg. 6.25h) per night depending on weight, exercise, season, etc.! What ChatGPT says about this ↑ Prompt: Why does the amount of sleep I need change depending on how much I weigh / whether I'm actively gaining or losing weight / the season? I'm a bodybuilder who bulks and cuts 20+ pounds per year, peaking in Jan (when I need the most sleep at 7+ hours) and at my lowest in the summer (when I only need like 5.5h) Your changing sleep needs are influenced by a combination of physiological, metabolic, and environmental factors related to your bodybuilding routines and seasonal rhythms. documents.label: Getting Back On Track
documents.body: After travel, an outstanding weekend, or something else that kicks me off my normal routine, I’ve developed a simple strategy to get back on track. My top priority is always to get back to my normal sleep schedule. In fact, I’ve even done 12-hour schedule flips (US ↔ India) without any jet lag whatsoever. How? Using supplements to modulate alertness: caffeine as an extender, the sleep stack with melatonin as a light switch. Take the time to learn how your body reacts to both and how you can then use them as tools to get back on track after disruption! For me, I find that once I get back into my normal sleep routine and have those first 4 hours in the morning to grab full control of my schedule that the rest falls back into place rather quickly 😄

documents.label: At a Glance
documents.body: Origin story: It all started back in college when I read https://books.chappyasel.com/7-habits-of-highly-effective-people and wrote my first personal mission statement. Since then, I’ve gone through 20+ iterations – honing in on a system molded to how my brain works! documents.label: Planning & Review Cycles
documents.body: Note on methodology: Plans are worthless, but planning is everything! The plan itself is only a temporary snapshot. The value comes from surfacing assumptions, confronting tradeoffs, exploring possibilities, and deciding what evidence would change my mind. I don’t want planning to reinforce my existing narrative or narrow my perspective. I use it to challenge that narrative, seek outside perspectives, and think divergently + critically enough to generate / uncover radically different options. Done well, planning actually increases my range and openness to change! Having already considered more possibilities also lets me recognize and move decisively when life presents a better one. If you add up all the planning cycles below you get ~5.9% of total time spent doing deliberate planning / strategy. I expect emergent planning through unanticipated opportunities to bring the real total closer to 10%. This is in line with best practice / what studies show is optimal for the explore exploit tradeoff! ♾️ Deep Think Weeks (72h) → annual foundations / direction / systems review + reset Inspired in part by Bill Gates’ Think Weeks (and my own inability to sit on my hands during “vacation” 😅), I started doing Deep Think Weeks (DTWs) in 2024! For at least one week annually, I completely divorce myself from normal work and routines to read + write + think deeply. No comms, meetings, social media (or really any media at all beyond books), or day-to-day work. Inhabit an entirely different headspace achievable only through this commitment to prolonged separation. I use this distance to think about the past and the future more clearly, audit the whole system (above and below), gather feedback, make a few very important decisions, and return with new ideas and experiments to run. It’s also a great time to reset + recharge + practice gratitude! ♾️ DTW26 RAPID RECAP ♾️ I dedicated 130+ hours across 15 days (Aug 25th-Sep 8th ‘26) to Deep Think Week this year. See above and below for context. I’ll do a full writeup / blog post in the coming days and will link it here but a rapid recap will have to suffice in the meantime… This one felt particularly consequential. With AGI on the near-term horizon, I wanted to fully step outside the bubble I’m so entirely immersed in the other 350 days of the year and regain some perspective. My info diet was almost entirely books about the history of computers + AI and about life + career (notes at https://books.chappyasel.com/). I’ve never before had this much uninterrupted time + space to think this intensively about the future + my life and work. I suspect very few are ever fortunate enough to! I’ll save most of what came out of those 130+h for the full writeup but here’s my most important conclusion… If you’re reading this, you’re probably at / near the frontier of all this too. We are living through a rare period – greater than the internet and the industrial revolution – when a relatively small number of people and ideas will disproportionately shape our shared future. This is no time to think small or to settle! Nor do I intend to. At the same time, the last few months have given me plenty of reasons for humility. I’ve made miscalculations, pursued false starts, overestimated some things, underestimated others, and spent important time moving in directions that ultimately weren’t right. It revealed weaknesses in how I think, work, and lead. It’s uncomfortable, but also one of the most valuable things this period has given me. Ambition has a way of exposing the places you need to grow! I’m leaving DTW26 with more questions and considerably less certainty in some previous answers – but also with a renewed perspective, a much better sense of what matters, and a feeling that a lot of previously disconnected pieces are finally clicking into place. I have the extraordinary privilege of refusing to compromise on spending my life working towards things I genuinely believe could matter at the scale of our shared future. I expect many more wrong turns, failed experiments, and hard lessons. But I would like to stay on that course… and now with a clearer compass than ever before. Rome was not built in a day, and neither am I or the work I hope to do. Onwards and upwards!! The process… Divergent thinking: Let my mind wander in random directions. Relaxed attention. documents.label: Considerations
documents.body: How much systemization should you apply to life? As with all things, the answer is certainly somewhere in the middle! No life vision leads to a directionless random walk. Holding onto a vision too tightly leads to stubbornness in the face of overwhelming contrary evidence. Too little routine prevents compound returns; too much creates rigidity. Too little perspective traps you in the urgency of the present; too much becomes paralyzing. Your own unique answer to ↑ defines your “style of thinking” / taste! Honing this is a lifelong pursuit. Above is a personal experiment built for my brain, my current responsibilities, and an unusually high appetite for structure. Here are the failure modes I’ve identified and am trying to watch out for: ⚙️ The system itself becomes the work 🪢 Decision latency cost of complexity 📐 Metrics distort what matters 🌀 Reflection becomes rumination ❓ Not every question needs an answer 🪤 Structure substitutes for self-trust 🧘 Systematic thinking crowds out intuition and relaxed attention 🌊 Consistency becomes resistance to change 🌱 Not every failure should be engineered away 🍀 Optimization crowds out serendipity 🤝 People don’t fit neatly into systems 🤖 A perfectly managed life stops feeling human

documents.label: Tips for Getting Started
documents.body: What I've seen work with my friends is starting as small as possible. A 10-second Daily Scorecard gives you a streak + real evidence and the one-sentence note gets you in the habit of reflecting. 7 Habits of Highly Effective People is where I'd go next for Weekly planning + a personal mission. The 12 Levers is my favorite map for choosing small, controllable techniques that change behavior. #️⃣ Log a Daily Scorecard. Take 10 seconds at the end of every day; after a few weeks, you have real data to ask why some days go better than others. Day Quality: Subjective overall quality from -2 to +2 Note: ≤10 words on what most shaped the day 📆 Add a Weekly. Once you have seven daily rows, spend 20 minutes reviewing the pattern + choosing the next week. Review: What explains the highs + lows? Choose: One #1 outcome for next week Schedule: Put the first steps on the calendar 🧪 Pick one lever. Use a recurring pattern from the Daily + Weekly to choose one Weekly Tweak. Technique: Specific / repeatable / controllable Experiment: Test for one or two weeks / measure / adopt, iterate, repeat, or drop 🧭 Write one page of direction. Once the loops are real, give them something to serve. Mission: What you intend to contribute Current Chapter: What this season is principally about Outcome: One observable result that would make the next month worthwhile Non-Priority: One attractive thing you are deliberately not funding 🥞 Earn the next layer. Add structure when the simpler loops expose a recurring gap. Monthly: Catch drift + make one correction Quarterly: Reset strategy + outcomes + allocation + active work Yearly / DTW: Reopen foundations + direction + the system itself Domain Systems: Build where the same problem keeps returning

documents.body: How does a shy nerd boy from high school find himself flexing on stage in front of hundreds of spectators donning little more than a G-string? Spray tanned and shaved from head to toe, I strode in front of the blinding spotlights as my name bellowed out over the PA system. Preparing to perform my solo posing routine, I masked first time jitters with a composed facade after hearing judges could sense fear like sharks smell blood in the water. Performing at a bodybuilding competition almost naked in front of a mass of ogling strangers was the culmination of a five-year journey. Once terrified at the mere thought of presenting a powerpoint in front of a small class, it hit me: how did I get here? I have been enthralled by computers and programming for as long as I can remember. Spending entire weekends squirreled away in my room, I taught myself how to write iOS applications, tinkered with Arduinos and bread board circuits, built custom computers, and reverse engineered electronic toys.
